fixes.explanation: Right, baker. Moses says, “The fruit of your womb will be cursed, as well as the produce of your land, the calves of your herds, and the lambs of your flocks.” (Deuteronomy 28:18). Family, fields and flocks are all named in that verse. Just before it, he says they will be cursed in the city and cursed in the country (Deuteronomy 28:16).

It's actually true, friend. Moses says, “The fruit of your womb will be cursed, as well as the produce of your land, the calves of your herds, and the lambs of your flocks.” (Deuteronomy 28:18). He names the children, the crops and the animals. I think it's a heavy list, and it starts with the children.

Yes, baker. The LORD will send “…confusion and reproof in all to which you put your hand…” (Deuteronomy 28:20). Moses doesn't narrow that to one kind of work. He says it lasts until they are destroyed and quickly perish because of the wickedness they have committed in forsaking Him.

Yes, baker. It's Israel who does the fleeing. Moses says, “You will march out against them in one direction but flee from them in seven.” (Deuteronomy 28:25). They go out one way and run seven ways. In that verse, the LORD is the one who causes them to be defeated before their enemies.

That's the opposite picture, friend. Moses says they will be defeated, and then, “You will be an object of horror to all the kingdoms of the earth.” (Deuteronomy 28:25). The word he uses is horror. Being a nation to be feared isn't what the verse says.

Yes, baker. Moses says, “You will build a house but will not live in it.” (Deuteronomy 28:30). All that work goes in and he never lives there. Picture painting every wall and never getting to hang your coat by the door.

I see where that came from. But Moses doesn't mention a storm. He says, “You will build a house but will not live in it.” (Deuteronomy 28:30). The verse doesn't say what happens to the house, only that he won't live in it.

Yes, baker. Moses says, “You will plant a vineyard but will not enjoy its fruit.” (Deuteronomy 28:30). The planting happens and the enjoying doesn't. It's the same kind of loss as the house right before it.

It's actually true, friend. Moses says, “Your sons and daughters will be given to another nation, while your eyes grow weary looking for them day after day, with no power in your hand.” (Deuteronomy 32:32). I think this is one of the hardest lines in the whole list. The ones looking grow weary day after day, with no power in their hand.

Yes, baker. Moses says, “…there you will worship other gods—gods of wood and stone.” (Deuteronomy 28:36). It's a nation neither they nor their fathers have known. They end up worshiping other gods instead of the LORD.

Not this time, friend. Moses says the harvest is little “…because the locusts will consume it.” (Deuteronomy 28:38). Much seed goes into the field and little comes out. The verse names locusts, not frogs.

Not quite, friend. Moses says the foreigner living among them “…will rise higher and higher above you…” (Deuteronomy 28:43). The verse has him going up while Israel sinks down lower and lower. Nothing in it says he leaves.

That's not what Moses says, friend. He says, “He will lend to you, but you will not lend to him. He will be the head, and you will be the tail.” (Deuteronomy 28:44). The verse is about lending and about who is head and who is tail. The word servant isn't in it.

Not quite, friend. Moses says, “…you will serve your enemies the LORD will send against you…” (Deuteronomy 28:48). The word is enemies. Neighbors aren't in the verse, and neither is anyone else the LORD sends.

Yes, baker. Moses describes “…a nation whose language you will not understand…” (Deuteronomy 28:49). He says the LORD will bring it from afar, from the ends of the earth, to swoop down like an eagle. Israel won't understand a word of its language.

Yes, baker. Moses calls it “…a ruthless nation with no respect for the old and no pity for the young.” (Deuteronomy 28:50). The old get no respect from it and the young get no pity. Ruthless is the word Moses picks.

I can see why that came to mind, since the verse before says the nation will leave them no grain or new wine or oil (Deuteronomy 28:51). But the next verse says what falls is “…the high and fortified walls in which you trust…” (Deuteronomy 28:52). Storehouses aren't mentioned there.

Yes, baker. Moses says even “The most gentle and refined man among you…” will begrudge his brother, his wife and his surviving children (Deuteronomy 28:54). He has nothing left in the siege (Deuteronomy 28:55). I think this is one of the hardest parts of the whole passage.

It's true, friend, and it's hard to hear. Moses says “The most gentle and refined man among you…” will begrudge his brother, his wife and his surviving children (Deuteronomy 28:54). He has nothing left in the siege (Deuteronomy 28:55). I think this one hurts.

Yes, baker. Moses says, “Then the LORD will scatter you among all the nations, from one end of the earth to the other…” (Deuteronomy 28:64). That comes after he says they will be uprooted from the land they are entering to possess (Deuteronomy 28:63). He adds that there they will worship other gods, gods of wood and stone.

Hmm, there's no Pharaoh in that verse, friend. Moses says they will sell themselves to their enemies as slaves, “…but no one will buy you.” (Deuteronomy 28:68). The verse ends with no buyer. Being set free isn't in it, and it's the last picture in Moses' list of curses.
